# Shepherd of Hermas Chapter 114 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Athous, Shepherd of Hermas 114 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/SHE_114_page_001.jpg

---

## Similitude 10, Chapter 4 — Final Words

**1** After some days I saw the shepherd again and asked him once more about these things. **2** He said to me: "I have already told you all the things I was sent to deliver; but because you inquire diligently, I will add one more thing. **3** Repentance for the servants of God — this must be proclaimed throughout all the world; for the Lord, in his compassion, has extended the season of repentance. **4** And God did not appoint his Son and the glorious angels to watch over the small and insignificant; rather, they watch over the great and the powerful who serve him in righteousness. **5** You must proclaim these things to all; and to all who have repented, speak words of encouragement so that they may not grow weary under the afflictions they endure for the name of the Lord. **6** For the afflictions they suffer are not purposeless; they have been appointed for the servants of God, that through them they may be purified and found worthy of the Lord." **7** "And tell also the leaders of the church: do not be double-minded in your prayers; for the Lord is not double-minded, and he hears all prayers and fulfills them." **8** "But will he truly fulfill them?" I asked. "He will," he said, "and if there is any delay, wait patiently; for the Lord does not delay because he is indifferent to you, but because he is long-suffering toward you, so that not one of you may be lost." **9** After these words he departed from me, and I saw him no more.

---

### Translator's Note
This final chapter of the Shepherd of Hermas ends on its most profound theological note: God's long-suffering patience, extended because he wishes none to perish (a close parallel to 2 Peter 3:9). The anti-double-mindedness command to church leaders in v. 7 — "do not be double-minded in your prayers" — ties the entire work back to its signature theme. "I saw him no more" is one of the simplest and most final endings in early Christian literature — a quiet departure that leaves Hermas, and the reader, alone with the call to repentance. SOPHIA follows LOGOS throughout.
